title: Demonetisation
summary: Overnight withdrawal of ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes, ~86% of currency in circulation by value, with a limited window to deposit or exchange.
claimAtLaunch: Elimination of black money held as cash, destruction of counterfeit currency, and cutting off terror financing. As returns approached 100%, the official justification shifted toward digitisation and formalisation.
whatHappened: The RBI's Annual Report 2017-18 confirmed 99.3% of demonetised notes returned to the banking system — ₹15.31 lakh crore of ₹15.41 lakh crore, with only ~₹10,720 crore unreturned. Counterfeit detection was minuscule. Currency in circulation collapsed, then recovered past pre-demonetisation levels (₹18.03 lakh crore by end-March 2018). The Supreme Court upheld the process 4-1 in January 2023, with a dissent questioning it.
assessmentNote: CORRECTED 2026-08-05 (adversarial triage 2): this record carried a failure verdict with NO stated reasoning, which is the one thing a scored record may not do. THE GROUND FOR THE VERDICT IS NARROWED TO WHAT IS MEASURED HERE. Four objectives were announced. Two are measured in this record and both fail on the government's own sources: the extinguishment of black money held as cash, against which 99.3 per cent of the notes returned to the banking system on the RBI's own count, so either little was held in cash or it was laundered and the premise was wrong either way; and the destruction of counterfeit currency, against which detection was minuscule. The other two are NOT part of the ground for this verdict and are entered below as unmeasured: the effect on terror financing, and the digitisation and formalisation objective that replaced the original justification as returns approached 100 per cent. The caseAgainst previously asserted failure "against every objective stated at announcement"; that sentence overstates what this record measures and is left standing only because it is a case, not a finding - the verdict now rests on the two objectives with evidence. THE WITHDRAWN WORDING IS NOT QUOTED HERE BECAUSE THERE IS NONE: this field did not exist before the correction, which created it rather than replacing anything. A correction of an absence says that it is one.

unmeasured.what: The effect of demonetisation on terror financing
unmeasured.why: Named as a founding objective and never measured in this record. The quantity is counterfactual - financing that would have occurred absent the measure - and no agreed definition of it exists, so it could not be collected even in principle. Incident counts published by the Union are not a measure of financing, and no retrieved source attributes a change in either to the note withdrawal.

unmeasured.what: The share of the growth in digital payments and tax filings attributable to demonetisation
unmeasured.why: Digital payment volumes and filing counts are published, so the aggregates exist; what does not exist is the counterfactual against which the increment could be attributed. This record's own caseAgainst concedes the point - digital adoption was already on a rising trend, so the incremental gain is unquantified. The objective also postdates the announcement, having replaced the original justification as returns approached 100 per cent, which is recorded here rather than treated as an original aim.

caseFor: Digital payments adoption accelerated sharply and durably, seeding the UPI infrastructure that is now genuine world-leading public infrastructure. Income-tax filings rose, and deposit data gave authorities analytics leads on suspicious accounts that conventional enforcement would not have produced. A one-time shock was arguably the only way to force behaviour change in a cash-preferring economy.
caseAgainst: It failed against every objective stated at announcement. Near-total note return means either little black money was held as cash or it was successfully laundered; either way the premise was wrong. Counterfeit seizures were trivial. The informal economy and small business absorbed severe disruption with no offsetting gain, and cash returned to above prior levels within eighteen months. Digital adoption was already on a rising trend, so the incremental gain is unquantified. Deaths occurred in queues.
shockExposure: None external — this is a rare clean case where the policy is not confounded by a global shock. The confound is internal: GST followed eight months later, making the two reforms' effects hard to separate through 2017-18.

title: Goods and Services Tax
summary: Replacement of a fragmented web of central and state indirect taxes with a single destination-based GST, governed by a GST Council with the Centre holding one-third of voting weight and states two-thirds, decisions requiring a 75% majority.
claimAtLaunch: One nation, one tax — a unified national market, simpler compliance, higher revenue buoyancy, and formalisation. States were guaranteed compensation for 14% annual revenue growth for five years.
whatHappened: Launched with four slabs plus cess rather than the single-rate ideal. GSTN technical failures, compliance burden and delayed exporter refunds marked the first years. Collections grew steadily to a record ₹22.08 lakh crore in FY2024-25 (+9.4% YoY), with a record single month of ₹2,36,716 crore in April 2025. Compensation ended June 2022 amid continuing state demands. The arc of that guarantee - its terms, its rupture in 2020, the cess that outlived it, and the Council's disposal of the extension request - is carried at L-0158 to L-0161 and is not restated here. GST 2.0, effective 22 September 2025, collapsed the structure to 5% and 18% plus a 40% demerit rate, with ~₹48,000 crore estimated revenue foregone.
assessmentNote: Written 2026-08-05 (adversarial triage 3); this record previously carried a verdict with no stated reasoning. FOUR THINGS WERE PROMISED AND THIS RECORD MEASURES TWO. Measured: revenue, which grew to a record 22.08 lakh crore in FY2024-25, and the registrant base, which passed 1.51 crore. Not measured here: revenue BUOYANCY, which the case against says was 'never clearly met' without giving a figure, and compliance cost, which is asserted to have fallen hardest on smaller firms and is nowhere quantified. Both are entered below as absences. Partly rests on what IS established: a constitutional amendment and a functioning federal tax council exist where two decades of attempts had failed, and interstate checkposts went; against that, the design carried four slabs for eight years and was rationalised in 2025, which is the government's own admission that the original structure was wrong. A caution about the registrant figure, on the same distinction another record in this corpus draws for payroll data: 1.51 crore registrants measures REGISTRATION, not formalisation, and this record does not treat the two as the same. The compensation arc is deliberately not restated here.
caseFor: A genuine unified market replaced checkpost-ridden interstate trade; e-way bills cut logistics friction measurably. Collections proved resilient and buoyant enough to absorb the 2025 rate cuts. The taxpayer base expanded past 1.51 crore active registrants. Achieving a constitutional amendment and a functioning federal tax council at all is a real institutional accomplishment that eluded two decades of prior attempts.
caseAgainst: Eight years of four-slab complexity, classification litigation and compliance cost fell hardest on MSMEs — the rationalisation to two slabs in 2025 is an admission the original design was wrong. The 14% buoyancy promise was never clearly met. States surrendered fiscal autonomy permanently in exchange for a guarantee that expired, and the COVID-era compensation dispute showed the Centre would restructure the bargain unilaterally under stress. And there was no forum in which to contest it: sixteen members asked the Council to extend compensation and its minutes record no decision on the request, while the dispute-resolution mechanism Article 279A(11) obliges the Council to establish has never been established at all.
shockExposure: COVID (2020-22) severely distorts the revenue trajectory and precipitated the compensation dispute; separating GST design effects from pandemic effects in FY21-FY22 is not cleanly possible.

unmeasured.what: Revenue buoyancy under GST against the 14 per cent growth the guarantee assumed
unmeasured.why: The case against asserts the buoyancy promise was never clearly met and gives no figure; this record carries collections in levels, not a buoyancy ratio against a base. The Department of Revenue and the GST Council between them hold the series needed to compute it. Entered 2026-08-05 when the assessment note was written and the claim was found to be argued without a measure.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A Department of Revenue or GST Council statement of buoyancy by year against the pre-GST base, or the underlying revenue and nominal-GDP series on a consistent definition.

unmeasured.what: Compliance cost borne by taxpayers, and its distribution by firm size
unmeasured.why: The claim at launch was simpler compliance and the case against holds that cost fell hardest on smaller firms. Neither is quantified anywhere in this record. No official estimate of GST compliance cost by firm size was retrieved.
unmeasured.wouldFill: An official or peer-reviewed estimate of compliance cost by turnover band.

sources.name: PIB, record gross GST collection FY2024-25

title: Corporate tax rate cut
summary: Base corporate tax cut from 30% to 22% (effective ~25.17% with surcharge and cess), and to 15% for new manufacturing companies.
claimAtLaunch: Improved after-tax returns would trigger a private investment revival and support Make in India by making Indian rates internationally competitive.
whatHappened: Revenue foregone of approximately ₹1.45 lakh crore per year, which PRS Legislative Research puts at about 5.2% of the FY20 revenue estimate. Private capital expenditure did not revive. Corporate profitability reached multi-year highs — Nifty-500 profit-to-GDP around 4.6% in FY24, the highest since FY08 — while private investment stayed weak. Firms directed the windfall largely toward deleveraging and share buybacks.
assessmentNote: Written 2026-08-05 (adversarial triage 3); this record previously carried a verdict with no stated reasoning. THE STATED OBJECTIVE IS MEASURED AND IT DID NOT OCCUR, WHICH IS THE WHOLE OF THE VERDICT. The cut was justified as triggering a private investment revival. Private capital expenditure did not revive, while corporate profitability reached multi-year highs - Nifty-500 profit to GDP around 4.6 per cent in FY24, the highest since FY08 - and firms directed the windfall largely to deleveraging and buybacks. Profits rising while capex does not is the signature of a windfall pocketed rather than deployed, and the cost is permanent and annual at about 1.45 lakh crore. THE COUNTERFACTUAL IS NOT MEASURED AND THE CASE FOR RESTS ON IT: COVID arrived six months after the cut, and investment responses to tax changes operate with long lags. That is entered below as an absence rather than dismissed. The verdict is asserted on the observed outcome over the period, not on a claim that the cut could not have worked in other conditions.
caseFor: It aligned Indian rates with regional competitors and repaired corporate balance sheets weakened by the twin-balance-sheet years, arguably a precondition for the later capex cycle. Investment responses to tax changes operate with long lags, and COVID arrived six months later — the counterfactual where the cut works absent a pandemic cannot be dismissed outright.
caseAgainst: The stated objective was investment revival and it did not occur; profits rose while capex did not, which is the signature of a windfall being pocketed rather than deployed. NIPFP research indicates corporate investment responds to capacity utilisation, competitiveness and credit availability — i.e. demand — not the tax rate, meaning the instrument was mismatched to the diagnosis. The cost is permanent and annual, and ~99.1% of firms were already near 25%, so benefits concentrated among roughly 4,700 large companies.
shockExposure: COVID arrived six months after the cut, permanently confounding clean attribution. However, the pre-COVID slowdown was already underway (FY20 growth 3.9%) and capex was already weak, so the pandemic cannot carry the whole explanation.

unmeasured.what: Private investment that would have occurred absent the rate cut
unmeasured.why: The case for rests on this and it cannot be observed: the cut preceded a pandemic by six months, and no counterfactual investment path exists or could be constructed from published data. The quantity has no agreed definition and could not be collected even in principle.

sources.name: Analysis of tax cuts versus private investment response

title: Flexible inflation targeting adopted
summary: Monetary Policy Framework Agreement (2015) and amended RBI Act (2016) established a 4% CPI target with a ±2% band and a six-member Monetary Policy Committee.
claimAtLaunch: A rules-based framework would anchor inflation expectations after the 9-11% inflation of 2010-2013.
whatHappened: CPI fell decisively into a 4%-centred range, with breaches during 2020 (COVID supply disruption) and 2022-23 (food and fuel following the Ukraine invasion). By mid-2026 CPI ran around 3.5-4.4%. The framework was renewed with the same 4%±2% target for April 2026 to March 2031.
assessmentNote:
RESCORED FROM worked TO contested, 2026-08-06, and contested rather than partly for a reason worth stating. The announced object of flexible inflation targeting was ANCHORING INFLATION EXPECTATIONS. What this record carries is lower CPI, the framework’s survival and its renewal through 2031. None of the three is a measure of expectations: CPI is the outcome expectations are supposed to influence, and institutional survival is evidence about the institution. partly would say part of the objective was achieved, which presupposes the objective was measured; it was not, so what the evidence supports is more than one defensible reading of the same facts — that the framework anchored expectations, and that disinflation arrived through commodity prices and global conditions with the framework alongside it. The record does not choose. THE SOURCING IS ALSO THE THINNEST IN THE CORPUS FOR A SCORED CLAIM: one T4 trade-press note on the renewal. The RBI’s own Inflation Expectations Survey of Households is the series that would settle this and it is not cited here.

PREVIOUS NOTE, PRESERVED VERBATIM: Written 2026-08-05 (adversarial triage 3); this record previously carried a verdict with no stated reasoning. WORKED IS ASSERTED ON THE ANNOUNCED OBJECT AND NOT ON ATTRIBUTION, and the distinction carries the verdict. The object was to anchor inflation expectations after the 9 to 11 per cent inflation of 2010-2013. CPI fell decisively into a 4 per cent-centred range, breached twice under identifiable external shocks, and the framework survived both, three governors and a change of political cycle without abandonment - then was renewed on the same target for 2026 to 2031. Institutional survival across shocks and renewal on unchanged terms is the strongest evidence available that expectations anchored. WHAT IS NOT MEASURED IS HOW MUCH OF THE DISINFLATION THE FRAMEWORK CAUSED. The case against is that the 2014-16 oil collapse handed much of it over, and that is not resolvable from anything retrieved; it is entered below as an absence. A reader should take this verdict as saying the framework held and was renewed, NOT that it produced the disinflation on its own. The 2024 CPI rebasing, which lowers the food weight, is also noted in the case against as making future performance flattering by construction.
caseFor: The clearest institutional success of the period. Inflation expectations anchored, the framework survived two major shocks and three governors without abandonment, and its renewal for a further five years reflects cross-party and market acceptance. Real interest rates turned positive, supporting financial savings.
caseAgainst: The disinflation was substantially handed to the framework by the 2014-16 oil price collapse, a windfall no policy earned; the framework's independent contribution is therefore overstated by the raw before-and-after comparison. The 2024 CPI rebasing lowers the food weight, which will dampen measured volatility going forward and makes future performance flattering by construction. Institutional autonomy in the surrounding period was contested — see the RBI autonomy record.
shockExposure: The 2014-16 oil collapse is a large positive confound at the start; COVID and the 2022 commodity shock are negative confounds mid-period. Peers faced the same commodity shocks, so peer-relative inflation performance is the fairer test.

unmeasured.what: The share of the post-2014 disinflation attributable to the framework rather than to the 2014-16 oil price collapse
unmeasured.why: The case against turns on this and no decomposition exists in anything retrieved. Separating a policy regime's contribution from a contemporaneous terms-of-trade windfall requires a counterfactual path for which no agreed construction exists.

title: Oil windfall capture through excise increases
summary: During the global oil price collapse the government raised excise duty on petrol and diesel nine times, capturing most of the terms-of-trade windfall for the exchequer rather than passing it to consumers.
claimAtLaunch: Framed as fiscal prudence — using a temporary windfall to consolidate rather than fund consumption.
whatHappened: Total excise on unbranded petrol rose from ₹9.48/litre (May 2014) to ₹19.48, and diesel from ₹3.56 to ₹15.33. Central petroleum-sector taxes rose from ₹1.72 lakh crore (FY15) to ₹4.92 lakh crore (FY22), a 186% increase over seven years.
caseFor: It funded fiscal consolidation and the capex push without new borrowing, converting a windfall that would otherwise have been consumed into public assets. Retaining high fuel taxes also served climate and current-account objectives by suppressing import demand. Passing the windfall to pump prices would have been reversed painfully when oil recovered.
caseAgainst: It transferred a consumer windfall to the exchequer during a period of weak household demand, and fuel taxes are regressive, falling hardest on transport-dependent low-income households. It contributed to the shift in the tax mix toward indirect taxation. When oil later rose, the duties were only partly unwound, so the burden persisted.
shockExposure: Entirely shock-driven — the policy exists only because of the 2014-16 global oil collapse, which was external and unearned. Peers who are net oil importers received the same windfall and made different choices.

title: Make in India and the 25% manufacturing target
summary: Flagship programme to raise manufacturing's share of GDP to 25%, originally by 2022, later extended to 2025 and then reset to 2035 under the National Manufacturing Mission.
claimAtLaunch: Manufacturing would rise to 25% of GDP and create 100 million jobs, positioning India as a global manufacturing hub.
whatHappened: Manufacturing's share did not rise. World Bank data show it falling from 15.07% of GDP (2014) to 13.14% (2024). Over the same decade Bangladesh rose from 16.61% to 21.89% and Vietnam from 20.37% to 24.33%. The target was reset to 2035 in Budget 2025-26.
assessmentNote: Written 2026-08-05 (adversarial triage 3); this record previously carried a verdict with no stated reasoning. TWO TARGETS WERE ANNOUNCED AND THIS RECORD MEASURES ONE. The share target is measured and decisively missed: manufacturing fell from 15.07 per cent of GDP in 2014 to 13.14 in 2024, and the target was reset to 2035 - a thirteen-year extension, which is the government's own statement that it was not met. The peer panel removes the external-conditions defence, because Bangladesh rose from 16.61 to 21.89 and Vietnam from 20.37 to 24.33 over the same decade under the same global conditions. THE 100-MILLION-JOBS TARGET IS NOT MEASURED ANYWHERE IN THIS RECORD, and writing this note is what surfaced that. It is entered below as an absence. The verdict rests on the share target alone, which is sufficient on its own terms; a reader should not take it as a finding about employment.
caseFor: It durably shifted policy attention and state-level competition toward manufacturing, and specific segments — notably electronics and mobile assembly — grew substantially from a low base. Global conditions were hostile: trade growth slowed worldwide after 2014 and supply chains fragmented, so holding share might itself count as an achievement.
caseAgainst: The peer panel dismantles the external-conditions defence: Bangladesh and Vietnam raised manufacturing share substantially over exactly the same decade under the same global conditions. India's share fell. The target was missed, extended, missed again, and reset by thirteen years, which is the clearest stated-goal-versus-outcome failure of the period.
shockExposure: COVID disrupted 2020-22, but the trajectory was already flat before 2020 and peers recovered faster. The 2025-26 US tariffs are a genuine late headwind but postdate the failure.

unmeasured.what: Manufacturing jobs created against the 100 million announced
unmeasured.why: Announced alongside the share target and measured nowhere in this record. India has no employment series that isolates manufacturing jobs attributable to a policy programme, and the periodic labour force survey measures sectoral employment without attribution. Entered 2026-08-05 when the assessment note was written and the target was found to be unscored.

sources.name: Hudson Institute on manufacturing and PLI

title: Production Linked Incentive schemes
summary: Outlay-based production incentives across 14 sectors totalling ₹1.97 lakh crore, intended to build scale in domestic manufacturing.
claimAtLaunch: Incentivise scale manufacturing, substitute imports, and integrate India into global supply chains.
whatHappened: Only ₹23,946 crore — about 12% of envisaged disbursement — was paid out by September 2025 (FY23 ₹2,968 crore, FY24 ₹6,753 crore, FY25 ₹10,112 crore). Electronics and mobile manufacturing was the clear success, with production up 146% between FY21 and FY25 to ₹5.45 lakh crore. Roughly 70% of recent disbursements went to electronics and pharmaceuticals; most other sectors underperformed, and reports suggest the scheme may not be extended.
assessmentNote: Written 2026-08-05 (adversarial triage 3); this record previously carried a verdict with no stated reasoning. THREE OBJECTIVES WERE ANNOUNCED AND THIS RECORD MEASURES ONE AND A HALF. Scale manufacturing: measured, and split - electronics and mobile production rose 146 per cent between FY21 and FY25 to 5.45 lakh crore, while only about 12 per cent of envisaged disbursement was paid out across five years and roughly 70 per cent of recent disbursement went to two sectors. That split is what partly rests on. Import substitution: NOT measured here at all, and entered below. Integration into global supply chains: measured only indirectly, through handset exports, and only for the sector that worked. The low disbursement is read here as evidence about the other sectors rather than about waste, because the schemes pay on verified output - unpaid money means unmet milestones. That reading cuts both ways and the record states both: it is also evidence that the diagnosis of what constrained those sectors was wrong.
caseFor: Electronics and mobile manufacturing is a genuine, large, verifiable success — India moved from assembly of last resort to a significant handset exporter within five years, which no prior industrial policy achieved. Low disbursement partly reflects the schemes' design working as intended: payment only on verified output, so unpaid money means unmet milestones rather than wasted money.
caseAgainst: Twelve percent disbursement across five years indicates most sectors could not meet thresholds, meaning the diagnosis of what constrained them was wrong. Concentration of benefit in two sectors suggests the successes were driven by specific global supply-chain shifts rather than the incentive design. Manufacturing's overall GDP share fell during the scheme's operation, which is the outcome that matters.
shockExposure: Launched into COVID, which disrupted early years but also drove the China+1 supply-chain shift that plausibly explains most of the electronics success — i.e. the shock may have caused the win rather than obscured it.

unmeasured.what: Imports displaced by production under the schemes, by sector
unmeasured.why: Import substitution was an announced objective and no figure for it appears in this record. Sectoral import series exist, but attributing a change in them to the incentive rather than to tariff changes, exchange rates or global supply shifts has no agreed construction, and no official estimate was retrieved.

title: RCEP withdrawal
summary: India withdrew from the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership at the final stage, the only one of sixteen negotiating countries to opt out.
claimAtLaunch: Cited unresolved concerns over trade deficits with eleven member states, a feared surge of Chinese imports, and inadequate safeguards for domestic producers.
whatHappened: RCEP proceeded without India. India subsequently pursued bilateral agreements instead: UAE CEPA (in force May 2022), Australia ECTA (December 2022), EFTA TEPA (in force 1 October 2025, carrying a US$100bn fifteen-year investment objective — L-0194 records that the Ministry calls it a "firm investment commitment" while the joint framing is an objective and an aim to "mobilise", and this record adopts neither word), the UK CETA (in force 15 July 2026, L-0204), and the EU agreement (negotiations concluded 27 January 2026, not in force, L-0205). CORRECTED 2026-08-05: this record previously described the TEPA commitment as binding and gave the China deficit as US$99.2bn in FY25 and about US$112bn in FY26 on a T4 source. That characterisation is withdrawn. The deficit figures are left out rather than restated, because the instrument now holds India-China trade on a calendar-year basis from both countries’ own submissions (L-0190, L-0191, P-119), and a financial-year figure from a newspaper cannot be set beside them — different period, different basis, and the two sides disagree in a way any single figure conceals. WITHDRAWN WORDING, quoted rather than paraphrased after the withdrawn-wording gate found this field describing what it withdrew instead of quoting it — the field previously read: "EFTA TEPA (October 2025, with a binding US$100bn fifteen-year investment commitment)" and "The trade deficit with China nonetheless widened to a record US$99.2bn in FY25 and about US$112bn in FY26."
caseFor: The stated fear was a Chinese import surge, and it happened anyway: on India's own submissions to UN Comtrade, imports from China reached US$149.495bn in calendar 2025 and were 19.86 per cent of India's total merchandise imports that year. Inside RCEP, with tariff elimination, the same pressure would have arrived against a lower tariff wall. India also retained the policy space it used — four agreements have entered into force since and a fifth is concluded, on terms negotiated bilaterally rather than accepted as a bloc schedule.
caseAgainst: India excluded itself from the world's largest trade bloc precisely as supply chains were being redrawn. The protection bought little on the measure that motivated the decision: RCEP entered into force on 1 January 2022 without India, and by calendar 2025 China supplied 19.86 per cent of India's merchandise imports, with India's total imports up 32.0 per cent on CY2021 against exports up 12.9 per cent. Staying out did not slow the import growth it was meant to slow, and the bilateral agreements that followed took until 2025 and 2026 to enter into force. Absence from the bloc also weakens India's position in regional rule-setting, which no bilateral agreement recovers.
shockExposure: Predates COVID by months; the pandemic then reshaped supply chains in ways neither side of the argument anticipated, making the counterfactual genuinely unknowable.

sources.name: UN Comtrade, India as reporter (699), partner China (156), flow M, HS TOTAL, annual 2025 — India-reported imports from China, US$149.495bn
UN Comtrade, India as reporter (699), partner World, flows X and M, HS TOTAL, annual 2021 and 2025 — the denominator for China's import share and the CY2021 baseline

assessmentNote: Written 2026-08-05 (phase 15 batch 13); this record carried a `contested` verdict with no stated ground, and `contested` is the value least able to explain itself. THE TWO LIVE READINGS ARE ABOUT A COUNTERFACTUAL, NOT ABOUT THE FACTS. Both cases accept the same figures: China supplied 19.86 per cent of India's merchandise imports in CY2025, imports rose 32.0 per cent on CY2021 against exports up 12.9. Reading one: the surge arrived anyway and would have arrived against a LOWER tariff wall inside the bloc, so withdrawal limited a harm that materialised regardless. Reading two: the protection bought little, since the surge arrived at full strength with the wall still standing, and the seat at the rule-setting table was given up for it. THE RECORD DECLINES BECAUSE THE EVIDENCE UNDERDETERMINES IT, and the underdetermination is structural rather than a gap in the retrieval: what separates the readings is what Chinese import growth WOULD have been inside RCEP, and no observation of a world India did not enter is available to anyone. This is the one of the five whose contest is EVIDENTIARY. It is not a case where the work was left undone — both sides rest on retrieved UN Comtrade submissions and the record's own figures.
revisitTrigger: Any published counterfactual estimate of India's import trajectory under RCEP accession terms, or an ex-post comparison against a member with a similar pre-accession tariff profile. Either would give the contest something to turn on other than assertion.

title: RBI autonomy episodes and surplus transfers
summary: A sequence of central-bank governance episodes: Raghuram Rajan not given a second term (2016), Urjit Patel's resignation (December 2018) amid Section 7 tensions, the Jalan committee's revised Economic Capital Framework, and escalating surplus transfers to the government.
whatHappened: The Jalan framework enabled a ₹1,76,051 crore transfer in 2019 — nearly triple the previous ₹65,896 crore record — followed by ₹2.11 lakh crore (FY24) and ₹2,68,590 crore (FY25, approved 23 May 2025, with the Contingent Risk Buffer raised to 7.50%). The FY25 transfer was aided by large foreign-exchange operations.
caseFor: Two governors departing over a decade is not itself evidence of capture, and both left for stated reasons that included personal choice. The surplus transfers followed a transparent, expert-committee framework rather than ad hoc demands, and the Contingent Risk Buffer was raised, not depleted — the RBI's balance sheet strengthened while transferring. Inflation targeting was preserved and renewed throughout, which is the substantive test of independence.
caseAgainst: The pattern matters more than any single episode: a non-renewal, a mid-term resignation over reserve and PCA disputes, an invocation of Section 7 powers never previously used, and a framework revision that unlocked record transfers. Growing fiscal reliance on RBI dividends blurs the monetary-fiscal boundary and creates an incentive for exchange-rate operations that generate transferable surpluses.

sources.name: NIPFP on RBI dividends as fiscal resource

title: COVID-19 contraction and fiscal response
summary: National lockdown from March 2020 produced a FY2020-21 contraction of about 5.8% (reported between -5.8% and -6.6% across revisions), followed by a 9.7% rebound in FY2021-22. The fiscal deficit spiked to 9.2% of GDP and general government debt peaked near 89%.
whatHappened: The contraction was among the deeper ones globally. China grew in 2020; Vietnam and Bangladesh stayed positive; Indonesia contracted mildly — indicating India's depth was substantially policy and lockdown-driven rather than purely pandemic-driven. Part of the FY21 deficit spike is an accounting artefact from bringing FCI food-subsidy dues on-budget in February 2021.
assessmentNote: Assessed contested on ground `criterion`: every figure here is agreed and the dispute is which frame governs. Neither side disputes the FY2020-21 contraction, the peer readings, the rebound or the deficit path; they disagree about whether a lockdown is judged by the time it bought a health system with very low per-capita infrastructure, or by a contraction deeper than peers facing the same virus. Nothing would settle that, which is what `criterion` records. THIS RECORD DOES NOT ADJUDICATE THE LOCKDOWN’S DESIGN and does not score the fiscal response against any stated objective; the case against’s reading that the depth points to lockdown design is a case, not a finding of this record. THE TYPE IS LEFT AS `shock` AND THE QUESTION IS OPEN, WRITTEN HERE RATHER THAN RESOLVED. Under operator Ruling 6 a chain of state decisions is not a shock, and under Ruling 7 a record is typed by its subject — but this record has two subjects, which its own title states: an external contraction and a domestic fiscal response. The two take different types on any answer, so no retype settles it, and the record’s own whatHappened ("India’s depth was substantially policy and lockdown-driven rather than purely pandemic-driven") cuts against the type it carries. THE CHOICE IS A SPLIT INTO TWO RECORDS OR A DECISION ABOUT WHICH SUBJECT THIS ONE IS, AND BOTH ARE MORE THAN A RETYPE. Recorded here so a later cycle inherits the question rather than rediscovering it; L-0064 and L-0027 were retyped in the same batch and this one deliberately was not.
caseFor: The lockdown bought time for health-system preparation in a country with very low per-capita health infrastructure, and free-grain distribution through PMGKAY reached hundreds of millions using existing NFSA rails — a delivery achievement few states of comparable income managed. The rebound was sharp, and consolidation from 9.2% to 4.4% within five years was faster than most peers.
caseAgainst: The contraction's depth relative to peers facing the same virus points to lockdown design, not the pandemic, and the four-hour notice period produced a migrant-worker crisis with severe human cost. Fiscal support was weighted toward credit guarantees over direct transfers, which supported balance sheets more than household demand and plausibly deepened the K-shaped recovery.
shockExposure: This record IS the shock. Peer comparison is the only clean lens: the shared exposure means India's relative depth isolates the domestic policy contribution.

title: US tariffs on Indian goods
summary: The United States imposed 25% tariffs on most Indian goods, then an additional 25% effective 27 August 2025 over India's Russian crude purchases, reaching 50% — the highest rate applied to any US trading partner.
whatHappened: Indian government estimates put roughly US$48bn of exports at risk; GTRI estimated around two-thirds of approximately US$87bn in US-bound exports were affected. CORRECTED 2026-08-04 against primaries retrieved that day. This record previously said the rate "was later cut to 18% under an interim arrangement" and that the Supreme Court "constrained" IEEPA-based tariff authority, and stated both as the current position; neither is right as written. The 18 per cent was a rate the 6 February 2026 United States-India joint statement said would be applied UNDER EXECUTIVE ORDER 14257. On 20 February 2026 the Supreme Court held in Learning Resources v. Trump that IEEPA does not authorise the President to impose tariffs at all — not that the authority was narrowed — and Executive Order 14389 the same day ended the duties imposed under every IEEPA order, including 14257 and 14329. India then paid ten per cent under a section 122 balance-of-payments surcharge from 24 February to 24 July 2026, and has paid ten per cent under a section 301 forced-labour action since. The instruments and their dates are held in L-0184 to L-0188; this record is the shock and its exposure estimates.
caseFor: The headline rate overstates the realised shock on the record's own figures. The 50 per cent peak held for months, not years: it ended entirely on 20 February 2026, when the authority it rested on was held not to exist, and the rate India has actually paid since has been ten per cent under two successive non-IEEPA statutes. The exposure estimates are gross rather than net - roughly US$48bn of exports at risk on the Indian government's own count against GTRI's two-thirds of about US$87bn in US-bound exports - and neither nets out re-routing, exemptions or substitution.
caseAgainst: For the period it ran, India faced the highest rate applied to any US trading partner, and the second tranche was imposed over India's Russian crude purchases rather than over any trade dispute, which makes the exposure political rather than merely commercial. India-specific severity is the part that does not wash out: every other shock in this instrument is shared with the peer panel and can be netted against it, and this one cannot, so it confounds every external-sector assessment for FY26 and FY27 whatever rate finally settles.
shockExposure: India-specific in severity, which makes it unusual — most shocks in this project are shared with peers. That specificity means it cannot be netted out via peer comparison and must be carried as a standalone confound for any FY26 and FY27 external-sector assessment.

title: Third GDP base-year revision to 2022-23
summary: MoSPI released a national accounts series rebased to 2022-23, using double deflation, a Supply-Use Table framework and new source data. It revised recent real growth up while lowering the level of nominal GDP by 3-4%.
caseFor: The methodology changed in a stated direction and the statement is primary: double deflation, a Supply-Use Table framework and new source data, set out in MoSPI's press note of 27 February 2026 and published with the release rather than reconstructed from it afterwards. That the basis is documented by the agency that made the change is the case for it, and on the sources retrieved it is the whole of the case.
caseAgainst: The revision arrived without a back-series, so there is no way to read the new basis against the old for any year before FY2023-24, and none of the three GDP regimes can be spliced. The direction of the two movements is convenient and unverifiable in the absence of that back-series: recent real growth was revised up while the level of nominal GDP was lowered by 3-4 per cent. The lower level moves every ratio-to-GDP in the instrument - fiscal deficit, general government debt, exports and gross fixed capital formation all step at 27 February 2026 with no change in underlying activity, an arithmetic step that reads as improvement.
shockExposure: None — but this record is itself a confound for every other macro assessment in the project, which is why it also exists as provenance record P-10.
